title: United States v. Cerebral Inc.
summary: Cerebral Inc., a digital mental health startup valued at $4.8 billion, entered into a nonprosecution agreement with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York. The company was investigated for policies and practices that encouraged the unauthorized distribution of controlled substances, specifically ADHD stimulants, from 2019 to 2022. Prosecutors alleged Cerebral sought to drive up profits by pushing clinicians to prescribe ADHD medications, using financial incentives and prescription metrics that did not consider medical appropriateness. The company agreed to forfeit $3.65 million and pay a $2.92 million fine (deferred). The company's founder/CEO Kyle Robertson was ousted in 2022, and Cerebral subsequently stopped prescribing controlled substances altogether.

commentary.comment: This case marks a significant regulatory action against a venture-backed telehealth startup, demonstrating that high valuations and investor backing do not shield companies from enforcement actions.
The nonprosecution agreement, rather than criminal charges, reflects Cerebral's cooperation and remedial actions including terminating its CEO and ceasing controlled substance prescriptions entirely.

Combined with an earlier $7 million FTC settlement for privacy violations and an additional $15 million FTC settlement for cancellation practices, Cerebral faces total regulatory penalties exceeding $28 million.

title: United States v. Mark Schena
summary: Mark Schena, 60, of Los Altos, California, president of Arrayit Corporation, was sentenced to eight years in prison and ordered to pay $24 million in restitution for defrauding investors and committing health care fraud. Schena falsely claimed to have invented revolutionary blood testing technology, orchestrated illegal kickbacks for unnecessary allergy testing, and attempted to capitalize on the COVID-19 pandemic with false claims about testing capabilities. Arrayit submitted over $77 million in fraudulent claims for COVID-19 and allergy testing. Schena was convicted by a federal jury on September 6, 2022.

category: Securities Fraud, Health Care Fraud, and Kickbacks

commentary.comment: This case represents a significant milestone as the first criminal securities fraud case related to the COVID-19 pandemic charged by the Department of Justice, highlighting the increased scrutiny on pandemic-related financial crimes.

The combination of securities fraud, healthcare fraud, and exploitation of the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrates the multifaceted nature of some fraud schemes, requiring coordination among multiple investigative agencies.

The involvement of a Silicon Valley executive in this fraud case may lead to increased scrutiny of medical technology startups and their claims, particularly those related to revolutionary diagnostic technologies.

title: United States v. Ruthia He and David Brody
summary: Ruthia He, founder and CEO of Done Global Inc., and David Brody, clinical president of Done Health P.C., were convicted in November 2025 in the DOJ's first criminal drug distribution prosecution against a digital health company. They exploited telemedicine rules during the COVID-19 pandemic to provide easy access to Adderall and other stimulants without legitimate medical purpose, generating over $100 million in revenue by arranging for the prescription of over 40 million pills. The scheme defrauded Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurers of approximately $14 million. Done used an 'auto-refill' policy allowing patients to obtain continued prescriptions after an initial encounter without any further interaction with a medical professional. The defendants were found guilty of conspiracy and unlawful distribution of controlled substances, as well as healthcare fraud. The case marks a watershed moment for telehealth enforcement.

commentary.comment: This case represents a significant milestone as the Justice Department's first criminal drug distribution prosecutions related to a digital health company using telemedicine, highlighting increased scrutiny on the intersection of technology and healthcare.

The exploitation of relaxed telemedicine rules during the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrates how public health emergencies can create vulnerabilities in healthcare systems that may be exploited by bad actors.

This case may lead to increased regulation and oversight of digital health companies, particularly those involved in prescribing controlled substances, potentially impacting the broader telemedicine industry.

title: United States v. Gary Cox (DMERx)
summary: Gary Cox, 79, CEO of DMERx, was sentenced to 15 years in prison and ordered to pay $452 million in restitution for orchestrating a $1 billion healthcare fraud conspiracy. Cox operated an internet platform that generated false and fraudulent doctors' orders for unnecessary medical items including orthotic braces and pain creams. The operation targeted hundreds of thousands of Medicare beneficiaries through misleading mailers and offshore call centers. Doctors signed orders without regard to medical necessity, based only on brief telephone calls or no interaction at all. Cox coordinated illegal kickbacks between telemedicine companies, pharmacies, and durable medical equipment suppliers. Medicare and insurers paid more than $360 million based on these fraudulent claims.

relatedLinks.text: 18 U.S.C. § 1349 - Conspiracy to commit health care fraud and wire fraud
42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b - Conspiracy to pay and receive health care kickbacks

commentary.comment: This case represents the largest healthcare software platform fraud by a single CEO, demonstrating how technology platforms can be weaponized to facilitate large-scale billing fraud across multiple states.
The 15-year sentence for a 79-year-old defendant reflects the severity with which courts treat systematic exploitation of Medicare beneficiaries through technology platforms.
The scheme's use of offshore call centers and misleading mailers targeting elderly beneficiaries highlights the intersection of traditional telemarketing fraud with modern healthcare technology.

title: United States v. Elizabeth Holmes and Ramesh 'Sunny' Balwani
summary: Elizabeth Holmes and Ramesh 'Sunny' Balwani were convicted for conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud for defrauding investors and patients through their company Theranos. They made false claims about Theranos's revolutionary blood-testing technology, its financial condition, and future prospects. Holmes was initially sentenced to 135 months (11+ years) in prison, but good conduct time has reduced her projected release to August 2032 - potentially serving just 66 months of her original sentence. She entered Federal Prison Camp Bryan in May 2023. Balwani was convicted on all counts and sentenced to 155 months. An appeal regarding convictions, sentences, and restitution orders was heard in June 2024. Holmes gave her first post-prison interview in 2025, maintaining her innocence.

relatedLinks.text: 18 U.S.C. § 1349 - Conspiracy to commit wire fraud

commentary.comment: This case highlights the potential dangers of 'fake it till you make it' culture in Silicon Valley startups, especially when applied to healthcare technology.
The significant prison sentences handed down may serve as a deterrent for other tech executives considering misleading investors or the public about their products' capabilities.
This case underscores the importance of rigorous scientific validation and transparency in medical technology development, and may lead to increased scrutiny of health tech startups.
